📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s mostly been the subject of Hollywood movies, but one day, an asteroid or comet could collide with Earth and cause serious damage. We don't have to look all that far back for an example. In 1908, in an incident now known as the “Tunguska Event,” a space rock, likely a few dozen meters wide, exploded over Siberia. Though scientists weren’t able to visit the site for another two decades, the landscape was still scarred from the explosion.

Astronomers predict that in mid-April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will fly by Earth. The 450-meter-wide body will miss us at a distance of only 19,000 miles. That’s about 12 times closer to us than the moon and much closer than many satellites. It will even be visible to the naked eye.

According to recent reports, in the past few decades, there’s been enormous progress in making these kinds of predictions. As space probes deepen our knowledge of small bodies in the solar system, astronomers have increasingly reliable and detailed data for finding potentially hazardous asteroids. Our ability to respond to such a threat, however, is another story. This is the missing and extremely important link—planetary defense technology that could allow us to deflect a dangerous object in time.

It has been revealed that in a sci-fi flick, such situations are often solved with a nuclear bomb. But in the real world, blowing up a big space rock into tiny bits is not ideal. Instead, it’s better to alter the asteroid's orbit. Everything in the vacuum of space is in motion. Our own planet travels about 20 miles every second. If the object hurtling towards us can be slowed down and thus reach the meeting point a little later, it will simply miss the Earth.

Four years ago, this was essentially what NASA tested on a pair of celestial bodies known as Didymos and Dimorphos. Astronomers at the Kitt Peak Observatory discovered Didymos, an asteroid measuring 780 meters across, 30 years ago. A few years later, Czech astronomer Petr Pravec observed that this asteroid had a “moonlet” orbiting it about every 12 hours. This smaller body, measuring about 151 meters in diameter, was then named Dimorphos.

The paired objects were a perfect testing ground for the kind of deflection a planetary defense system would involve. Locked in on these targets, NASA launched the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) in late 2021. Nearly a year later, the DART probe crashed into Dimorphos.

Scientists had hoped that the impact of the probe—which was barreling toward the asteroids at over 13,000 miles per hour—could shorten the period of the mini-moon's orbit by a minute or more. In the end, it was slowed down by 33 minutes. This major deviation was caused by the ejection of debris, leading to a much greater recoil than what was produced by the impact itself. In addition, the orbital speed of both asteroids around the sun also slowed. And in a sense, Dimorphos briefly became a comet—the debris released by the impact creating a long tail behind it.

It has been revealed that but questions remain about the longer-term impacts of this test. In October 2024, the European Space Agency (ESA) sent off the space probe Hera to rendezvous with both asteroids. After a flyby of Mars, the probe began its arrival phase this past October. It took its first image about 800 miles away, and the first detailed image of Didymos was published in early November.

Now in their vicinity, Hera will study both bodies in depth. Though there’s much we can learn about asteroids by observing them from our planet, nothing can replace close-up exploration, and this will be the first time a binary asteroid system will be explored in detail. One of the mission's goals is to find out how such asteroid pairs form. Didymos is also interesting for its rapid rotation, turning once every 2.3 hours—placing it on the very edge of stability.

But of course, beyond this traditional astronomy research, which could also take place at another set of binary asteroids, Hera will investigate the consequences of the DART mission. This will include studying the impact site. Because there are so many knowns about the impact itself, scientists can also use this opportunity to understand craters more broadly, answering questions such as whether the strength of the material or gravity plays a more decisive role in crater formation.

It has been revealed that hera will also determine the exact mass of Dimorphos, an vital detail in assessing the effectiveness of the DART mission as a test of planetary defense technology. The probe also contains a lidar instrument for mapping the asteroid's topography and instruments for investigating the chemical composition of the surface. Additionally, we can expect to see detailed images of the asteroids taken with a resolution of 1 meter per pixel.

In a recent development, the probe is also carrying two miniature, cube-shaped satellites, called “CubeSats” for short, which it will deploy in January 2027. In Earth’s orbit, CubeSats are often used for simple experiments, including student projects, and they can even be stacked together to create larger satellites.

Hera’s CubeSats, named Juventas and Milani, will attempt to land on the surface. Using radar capable of probing up to a depth of 100 meters, Juventas will focus on geophysical exploration of the asteroid Dimorphos. Additionally, a gravimeter on board will measure how the gravity on Dimorphos changes during its orbit due to the parent asteroid, Didymos. Meanwhile, Milani will carry out a detailed investigation of the asteroids’ surface composition and will search for traces of dust and the volatile substances contained within many space rocks.

According to current intends, this main phase of the Hera probe's mission is expected to last until the summer of next year, and findings from this probe will likely only become more relevant, not just as Apophis approaches, but even after it slings back into space. In the year 2000, we knew of only 300 near-Earth asteroids—those that approach Earth or directly cross its orbit. Today, we know of over 43,000.

Why Sony's fresh digital Walkmans cost thousands of dollars

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The numbers on Sony’s latest Walkmans raise some questions that the spec sheets don’t answer.
  • According to recent reports, some of us have never owned a Walkman, and judging by the sticker prices of the latest models, that may never change.
  • The implied explanation for those insane prices is the premium components and materials Sony uses across the models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The numbers on Sony’s latest Walkmans raise some questions that the spec sheets don’t answer.

According to recent reports, some of us have never owned a Walkman, and judging by the sticker prices of the latest models, that may never change. Sony never stopped making them, though, and on October 15 the firm opened pre-orders for three new models. The cheapest, the NW-ZX900, costs a staggering $1,899. The NW-WM1AM3 sits above it at $2,999, while the gold-plated NW-WM1ZM3 flagship will set you back almost six grand.

The implied explanation for those insane prices is the premium components and materials Sony uses across the models. And while those parts aren't cheap, they don't explain why both less-expensive models cost more than twice what their predecessors did. They also don't explain why the $5,899 flagship offers no significant improvement on paper over the NW-ZX900, with essentially the same output from the headphone amp and a shorter battery life, at up to 33 hours of hi-res playback. Nor do they explain why that flagship works out to about $3,800 in Japan once sales tax is taken out. It's clear Sony is selling these as luxury goods to a small audiophile market, but as with a lot of audiophile gear, the returns shrink fast as the price goes up.

In a recent development, the $5,899 WM1ZM3 flagship's main chassis is machined from 99.99 percent pure oxygen-free copper and then gold-plated. The previous flagship's aluminum rear panel gets swapped for a copper one, and even the screws get a low-resistance gold plating, which Sony claims gives a more stable ground connection and, in turn, stronger bass and a wider soundstage. Inside, there's thick Kimber Kable wiring borrowed from Sony's DMP-Z1 desktop player, a second large polymer capacitor and a copper block over the digital circuitry that's 34 percent heavier than before. All that metal weighs a hefty 670g (around 1.5 pounds), up from the 2022 model's 490g (around 1.1 pounds).

According to recent reports, the more modest $1,899 ZX900, meanwhile, has a machined aluminum chassis with a gold-plated copper rear panel, just like the $2,999 WM1AM3, and the same ultra-low-noise voltage regulator and crystal oscillators as its pricier siblings. All three use Sony's S-Master HX digital amp and are rated at 250mW per channel from the 4.4mm balanced jack, while storage goes from 64GB to 128GB to 256GB. So for the extra $4,000 between the ZX900 and the flagship, you're getting copper, better wiring, capacitors and more storage.

In its review of the $3,699 WM1ZM2, What Hi-Fi? pointed out that the (much) cheaper WM1AM2 shared most of the flagship's specs and engineering, and docked the ZM2 points for its limited power output. That's not addressed by the ZM3, either, since it's rated for the same 250mW per channel. AV Watch heard more of a step-up in transparency and space from the ZM2, but still called the AM2 excellent value for money. If an extra $2,300 paid for a difference that reviews couldn't agree on back in 2022, it's difficult to see how one could justify the $4,000 gap between the ZX900 and the ZM3 today.

Industry observers note that the NW-WM1Z, Sony's gold-plated Walkman from 2016, debuted at $3,199. In 2022, the WM1ZM2 became Sony's $3,699 Walkman for over-the-top audiophiles alongside a $1,399 WM1AM2. The ZX707 followed in 2023 at $899. This year, the WM1ZM3's price has jumped 59 percent, but both cheaper models have also more than doubled in price, meaning there's no longer a premium Walkman option under $1,000. Astell&Kern's Android-based SP4000 flagship, meanwhile, lists at $4,290, or about $1,600 less than the ZM3.

Retailers in Japan expect the WM1ZM3 to sell for around ¥655,000 and the ZX900 for around ¥215,000. Take out the 10 percent consumption tax that's included in Japanese shelf prices and convert at September's average of about ¥156 to the dollar, and that's roughly $3,800 and $1,250. In other words, US buyers are paying more than 50 percent more for the same players. Copper hit a record of around $14,850 a metric ton in August, but even a 670g (around 1.5 pounds) Walkman made entirely of copper would only contain about $10 worth of it.

Industry observers note that so if you're not already someone who will happily spend thousands on headphones and amps, the Walkman for you is still the NW-A306, which debuted at $349 in 2023 and is still on sale. The newly introduced trio replaces Sony's high-end players, not that one, and if you're set on one of them, the ZX900 gets you most of the flagship's hardware for the money. In essence, Sony has built all three Walkmans from expensive parts. But the jump in price since the previous generation looks like it has more to do with what die-hard audiophiles will pay for one, rather than what they cost to build.

Harbinger is building the unsexy EVs that keep the economy moving

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, while legacy automakers tap the brakes on electric vehicles, one startup is hitting the accelerator.
  • Harbinger is stacking up wins by skipping the consumer EV hype cycle altogether and focusing on the unglamorous workhorses that keep the economy running: Class 4–6 delivery vans and box trucks.
  • “We’re not solving the big obvious problem because everyone’s going to solve that problem, and as a result, the margins get kind of ground down to zero,” Harris indicates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, while legacy automakers tap the brakes on electric vehicles, one startup is hitting the accelerator. Earlier this month, electric truck maker Harbinger raised $240 million in a Series D round, capping a banner stretch that includes a $300 million order from FedEx and a latest defense contract with the US military.

Harbinger is stacking up wins by skipping the consumer EV hype cycle altogether and focusing on the unglamorous workhorses that keep the economy running: Class 4–6 delivery vans and box trucks. The manufacturer’s thesis is simple: go after the overlooked commercial segments where legacy trucks are weak and giant automakers can’t be bothered to compete, CEO John Harris tells me.

“We’re not solving the big obvious problem because everyone’s going to solve that problem, and as a result, the margins get kind of ground down to zero,” Harris indicates. “We’re solving problems that — they’ve just been there forever and you no longer think of this as a problem, you just think of it as like part of existence. It’s like a tax on your life.”.

Founded in 2021 by veterans of Canoo, QuantumScape, and Faraday Future, Harbinger aims to fill a structural gap in the auto market, in which most passenger EV platforms lack the durability to scale up while the heavy-duty platforms are too heavy and expensive to scale down.

“In auto, you have Class 1 companies and you have Class 8 companies,” Harris claims. “And everything in between is kind of a wasteland... It is much, much, much too small for a big organization to serve.”.

Recent findings suggest that which is not to say the industry hasn’t tried. Ford and GM both took shots at electrifying the medium-duty segment with the E-Transit and BrightDrop delivery vans, respectively, but sluggish sales and the loss of federal incentives forced them to discontinue or cancel those models.

Harris claims that major automakers are ill-suited to task, with their over-reliance on third-party suppliers to build all the necessary components. The effort becomes too spread out and expensive, with not enough return on your investment. That’s why Harbinger is attempting a more vertically integrated approach, he says, assembling its own battery packs and drive units in house — with inverters to follow.

“If you are not vertically integrated in auto, you don’t build viable products,” Harris states. “We believe that electric vehicles are only viable when they’re competitive on acquisition price with combustion vehicles.”.

Of course, Harris and his fellow cofounders have tasted failure in their previous ventures. Harbinger’s CTO Phillip Weicker cofounded EV startup Canoo, which ran out of cash and filed bankruptcy in 2025. Harris himself spent a year at tumultuous Chinese EV manufacturer Faraday Future before moving on to Xos Trucks and then Palmer Luckey’s Anduril.

“I was an engineer at Faraday. I wasn’t in charge of anything,” Harris says. “So it’s not like, ‘John, why did Faraday not succeed?’ I can tell you lots of reasons, but it wasn’t because the plastic part that I designed didn’t work. It was because the plastic part that I designed was going into a vehicle for which the world customer base was like three people.”.

Those companies “fundamentally didn’t work,” he adds, “because of the market fit concern and the leadership issue. Not because the engineering didn’t work or electrification wasn’t ready or they didn’t have enough capital.”.

According to recent reports, harbinger’s approach is more pragmatic, offering both battery-electric and plug-in hybrid powertrains for its medium-duty trucks. The manufacturer is not pursuing heavy-duty Class 8 trucks like the Tesla Semi, however, as Harris argues the economics of electric long-haul trucking are unworkable.

Sources indicate that “Class 8 electrification to me is one of those markets. I completely reject the notion that that’s a good fit for electrification for the majority of the market,” he says. “We can put [the Tesla Semi] on the watch list with the Cybertruck.”.

With companies like Amazon and FedEx making serious moves to secure more electric delivery vehicles, Harbinger is well-positioned to be a key supplier. And with diesel prices skyrocketing as a result of the war with Iran, more companies are waking up to a reality in which EVs can help bring down their costs.

Harbinger isn’t just building delivery trucks — it’s also branching into energy storage and military technology. For example, the company supplies battery power systems to Airstream and partners with American Rheinmetall and Forterra to build self-driving hybrid supply vehicles for the US Army. Harbinger also recently bought Phantom AI to bring advanced driver-assistance features to commercial fleets, in the hopes of giving companies a clear, measurable return on their safety investments.

Recent findings suggest that with millions in fresh capital and major contracts already on the books, Harbinger has cleared the first major hurdle that tripped up its founders’ past ventures. Now comes the hardest part in the auto business: proving it can actually build them at scale.

In a recent development, “Auto is a significant enough opportunity that it can get people’s attention,” Harris says. “It’s also punishingly difficult. So if you can make something that works in auto, it will be phenomenal in every other segment, because every other segment, the competition is essentially weaker.”.

#2554. SEC examines Nvidia’s accounting as its stock suffers worst run since 2008

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1353 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

SEC examines Nvidia’s accounting as its stock suffers worst run since 2008

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1353 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang at Village Global’s The Grove event in November 2023.
  • It has been revealed that the US Securities and Exchange Commission is examining Nvidia’s accounting, Reuters reported on Friday, citing two people briefed on the matter.
  • Industry observers note that the Upcoming York Times confirmed the investigation with its own sources.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang at Village Global’s The Grove event in November 2023.

It has been revealed that the US Securities and Exchange Commission is examining Nvidia’s accounting, Reuters reported on Friday, citing two people briefed on the matter. SEC enforcement staff are scrutinising potential accounting concerns at the manufacturer, they said. Nvidia’s shares fell 14% by the close.

Industry observers note that the Upcoming York Times confirmed the investigation with its own sources. One said it is at an early stage, and it may not lead to civil charges. The Wall Street Journal broke the news of the civil probe on Tuesday. Its scope includes whether Nvidia’s disclosures misled investors, the paper said.

According to recent reports, the SEC declined to comment to Reuters, and Nvidia did not respond to either outlet. Neither could say exactly which accounting problems are under review. Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing, Reuters noted, and many close without any enforcement action.

It has been revealed that both reports point to a change Nvidia made last year. It began reporting revenue by each customer’s headquarters instead of its billing address, and Singapore disappeared from its geographic breakdown.

Recent findings suggest that the NYT states Nvidia made the change after its October 2025 report on Megaspeed, the Singapore manufacturer where Alice Huang was an executive. Revenue booked through Singapore had surged 70% to $104bn when Nvidia stopped disclosing it, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday.

US authorities suspect Alice Huang is a Chinese spy, and China has denied it. Megaspeed says she left in August 2025 and that it conducted lawful business.

Friday was Nvidia’s seventh straight day of losses and its seventh straight weekly decline, the longest weekly losing streak since 2008, CNBC reported. The stock is down 46% over those seven weeks, about $2.6tn in market value. At roughly $3tn, Nvidia is now the world’s fourth most valuable company, behind Apple, Microsoft, and Alphabet.

In a recent development, about $1tn of that has gone since Jensen Huang left. Nvidia was worth $4.19tn at the close on 11 November, the day before it announced his departure. By Friday afternoon it had lost $1.04tn, Business Insider calculated from Bloomberg data.

Sources indicate that the slide began before the scandal, though, amid worries about AI spending and fresh chip competition from Google and AMD, CNBC noted. Not even Tuesday’s raised forecast stopped it.

The wider market fell too. The S&P 500 dropped 3.7%, which left it in a correction, more than 10% below its 6 October record. The Nasdaq Composite lost 5.3% and turned negative for the year. The PHLX Semiconductor Index fell 10.7%, The Associated Press reported. Anthropic, a day after its record listing, gave back 8.5%.

The affairs started the scandal, but Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying” were what moved Nvidia’s board, WIRED reported on Friday. It cited two people familiar with private discussions between the chair and other directors.

It has been revealed that board chair Harvey Jones has mentioned the board does not intend to reinstate Huang. It has hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate the circumstances of his resignation, the NYT reported.

Sources indicate that A separate NYT investigation describes decades of abuse of staff. It draws on more than a dozen current and former employees and court records spanning over 20 years.

Recent findings suggest that as Nvidia grew richer, Huang told groups of subordinates that money no longer motivated them, three people told the NYT. Humiliation, he mentioned, was the only way to get more work out of them. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, a witness said. He told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain”.

“I’d rather torture you into greatness, because I believe in you,” Huang once said in public, the NYT reported.

According to recent reports, nvidia settled with at least two former senior leaders who had raised concerns about his conduct in the mid-2000s. Michael Winston, a former head of human resources, threatened to sue in 2005 after he was fired. Nvidia reached a confidential settlement with him worth more than $1m, the NYT reported.

Huang’s conduct was “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he had witnessed in his career, Winston remarked when he threatened to sue.

A former manufacturer lawyer, Stephen Pettigrew, sued in 2007; Nvidia denied wrongdoing, and the case settled in 2009.

Huang’s spokesman, John Fisher, told the NYT that Winston’s allegations were “fabrications” from a fired employee. Nvidia declined to comment. Many staff still revere Huang, the NYT added, and thousands have signed a letter backing his return.

In a recent development, so does Donald Trump. At a press conference on Friday, the US president urged Nvidia to reinstate Huang.

“I’d like to see Jensen make a major apology and go back,” Trump said.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated on Sunday that he wanted more information about how Nvidia worked inside, the NYT reported.

“Were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” Bessent said.

Sources indicate that on Thursday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee’s Republican chair, Brian Mast, used export law to release licence data for Nvidia and AMD sales to China. Companies asked to sell 3.4 million AI chips there between December 2025 and May 2026. The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security approved more than 879,000, including sales to firms the Pentagon lists as Chinese military companies.

Recent findings suggest that the approvals covered 75,000 chips for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, Reuters reported. It is not clear how many of the approved chips were shipped. The chips were Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s equivalent, the MI325X.

Mast called two firms named in Nvidia’s applications, Maginfra and Fresh Matrix, “fake companies”, CNBC reported. Nvidia said the approvals came with strict conditions and limited volumes, and that it has since stopped shipping H200s to China. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC that Commerce appeared to approve about one request in four.

The data follows reports that a senior Commerce official rushed H200 approvals, and a congressional commission’s finding that China’s military is seeking Nvidia’s chips.

According to recent reports, three House Democrats, Jamie Raskin, Gregory Meeks, and Sydney Kamlager-Dove, are asking whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick blocked efforts to stop suspected chip smuggling while his family’s firm held Nvidia shares. Their letter to Cantor Fitzgerald’s chair, Brandon Lutnick, demands records of every Nvidia trade since January 2024.

Cantor held more than 3.5 million Nvidia shares before Lutnick became secretary, the lawmakers wrote. It later cut that holding by nearly half, and still held about $310m in Nvidia stock at the end of March. They also point to Bessent’s claim that four agencies backed blacklisting Megaspeed for months while Commerce held out.

In a recent development, A Cantor spokesperson called the claims inaccurate, Politico reported. The firm’s Nvidia holdings arise mainly from equity swaps it hedges for clients, she stated. Democrats cannot compel the records yet, but Raskin and Meeks will gain subpoena power when their party takes the House majority in January.

Sources indicate that the Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation plans to spend $350m renting computing time from CoreWeave, in which Nvidia is a major shareholder, Bloomberg reported, citing tax filings. It had already spent $108.3m.

Recent findings suggest that the foundation held $12.7bn at the end of 2025, almost 90% of it in Nvidia stock. CoreWeave said the computing goes to the foundation’s grant recipients for research. Bloomberg said the deal demonstrates how even tech billionaires’ charities are caught up in the AI industry’s circular financing. Nvidia’s own web of stakes and guarantees in its customers already runs to billions.

Huang is due to face three House committees in a closed-door interview on 1 December, as TNW reported. Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, follows on 2 December.

#2552. What are the actual differences between cheap and expensive sound systems?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1575 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

What are the actual differences between cheap and expensive sound systems?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spending more doesn't guarantee a better fit for you, though there are some clear differences as you climb in price.
  • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
  • Your TV's built-in speakers are fine...
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spending more doesn't guarantee a better fit for you, though there are some clear differences as you climb in price.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Your TV's built-in speakers are fine... if you don't care about hearing dialogue clearly, feeling the bass or knowing where an explosion is coming from. Even an inexpensive soundbar can make a noticeable difference.

According to recent reports, soundbars can range from around $100 to well over $1,000, as demonstrated by our picks for the best soundbars. Many highly rated models that provide good value fall between $200 and $600 in our findings, as well as those from other outlets like Consumer Reports. The options vary considerably in how they handle surround sound, from basic bars designed to improve dialogue to more elaborate systems with wireless subwoofers and rear speakers.

Diminishing returns are key here. The biggest improvements usually come from moving beyond TV speakers and entry-level soundbars. After that, you're paying for more capable hardware, additional features and refinements that may be less noticeable to the average listener. Let's look at a couple of different price buckets, which aren't exact quality dividers but will give you an idea.

In a recent development, A basic soundbar can make dialogue easier to hear and give movies more presence. Models under $100 are pretty stripped-down and have limited connectivity, fewer sound modes and can't reproduce deep bass. They're designed to improve everyday TV audio without needing a complicated setup.

In a recent development, at this price, you're typically looking at a 2.0 or 2.1 setup. If you're not familiar with speaker channel numbers, a 2.0 soundbar has two audio channels (stereo), while a 2.1 model adds a separate subwoofer to handle lower frequencies. The Hisense HS2100, for example, sells for around $120 and includes a wireless subwoofer that gives it a fuller sound than a standalone bar.

In a recent development, for just under $200, you can get considerably more hardware. The Hisense HS5100 is a 5.1-channel system (adding two rear speakers and a center channel compared to 2.1) with a dedicated subwoofer and satellite speakers. Instead of relying on processing to simulate surround sound, the rear speakers provide audio behind you. It doesn't support Dolby Atmos, though, so you don't get overhead effects.

This is where soundbars start offering more impressive improvements to your TV's audio. You should see features like eARC for sending audio to your soundbar from any other input, as well as Wi-Fi streaming and more robust app features like full EQ management. You might also get upward-firing drivers for Dolby Atmos, making compatible movie soundtracks more immersive. Exact features vary among models; for example, the Hisense AX3120Q is a 3.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar for around $280.

A 3.1.2 system has three front-facing channels, a subwoofer and two height channels. That gives you a dedicated center channel for dialogue and hardware designed to reproduce overhead effects. The Polk Signa S4 is another example for around $449, while Sony's Bravia Theater Bar 5 offers a less expensive $350 alternative with a dedicated subwoofer and 3.1-channel configuration, virtualizing the overhead and directional effects. Neither gives you separate rear speakers for physical surround sound.

Recent findings suggest that at the upper end of this price range, there are more complete surround systems with dedicated rear speakers and multiple height channels. The Hisense AX5140Q is a 5.1.4-channel system with a wireless subwoofer, two satellite speakers and four upward-firing drivers. It also includes features like a graphic equalizer, independent channel adjustments and dialogue enhancement. That's a lot more hardware than you'll find in a basic soundbar.

It has been revealed that in this range, you'll find more capable surround sound systems, but the improvements aren't just about adding more speakers. The Samsung HW-Q800F offers 5.1.2-channel audio with a wireless subwoofer and up-firing drivers for Dolby Atmos. It doesn't include rear speakers, though; it uses side-firing drivers for virtual surround effects. Other models, like Samsung's 3.1.2-channel HW-QS700F soundbar, offer features like automatic adjustments based on whether the bar is on a TV stand or a wall.

The JBL Bar 1000MK2 offers another step up. Its 7.1.4-channel configuration includes detachable, battery-powered satellite speakers, a subwoofer and upward-firing drivers. It also has room correction and a graphic equalizer. The detachable speakers give you physical surround sound when you want it, without having to keep them out permanently.

In a recent development, at the upper end of this range, you have systems like Marshall's $1,000 Dolby Atmos Heston 120 soundbar. But spending more doesn't necessarily mean getting a better fit for your room.

A dedicated home theater system gives you more control over where sound comes from. Instead of using a soundbar to simulate surround effects, an AV receiver sends audio to individual speakers around your room. A basic 5.1 setup includes left and right front speakers, a center channel, two rear surround speakers and a subwoofer.

The difference isn't just about having more speakers, though. A properly configured surround system can create a more convincing sense of space and make it easier to hear where dialogue and sound effects are coming from. But the difference between surround sound systems and soundbars indicates with tradeoffs in cost, space and setup complexity.

If you're willing to invest in separate components, a receiver-based system gives you more room to customize and upgrade later. Home Audio Advice put together a roughly $1,300 setup using a Yamaha RX-V4A receiver and a Klipsch Reference Cinema 5.1.4 speaker package. The receiver powers a basic 5.1 setup and the Klipsch package includes four additional height-effect speakers that can be used after upgrading to a compatible receiver. The flexibility is a major advantage.

However, soundbars are still able to offer a convincing surround experience. Samsung's 11.1.4-channel HW-Q990D soundbar is an example, though it doesn't come cheap. There are also modular options like LG's Dolby Atmos FlexConnect home theater system, which let you arrange compatible speakers around your room without committing to traditional wired placement.

One of the biggest differences between inexpensive and premium speakers is how accurately they portray the sound captured by media creators. A speaker with an uneven response may emphasize certain frequencies while making others harder to hear, while a more balanced frequency response produces a more natural sound.

Bass reproduction is another area where better equipment makes a noticeable difference. Low-frequency extension describes how deep a bass signal a speaker can play before it starts dropping off. Smaller speakers struggle with the lowest frequencies, which is why a subwoofer makes such a difference in a home theater.

Sources indicate that louder isn't necessarily better, but a system able to maintain sound quality at higher volume definitely matters. More capable speakers can deliver greater output while maintaining a more consistent sound, which is helpful in larger rooms or when listening at high volumes.

In a recent development, the jump from TV speakers to an inexpensive soundbar is usually a lot more noticeable than moving from a midrange to a premium one. Even soundbars under $300 can give a substantial improvement, and some budget models deliver sound quality that competes with more expensive options. Consumer Reports has found that certain less expensive soundbars rival pricier models in overall sound quality. Spending more isn't pointless, but the improvements become less direct as you move up the price ladder.

Sources indicate that at higher price points, you're typically paying for refinements instead of a completely different audio experience. Those improvements can matter if you have a large space, watch a lot of movies, are a serious gamer or want to customize your setup over time. But someone watching content that doesn't take advantage of modern audio features (like news and sports) in a small living room may not notice enough of a difference to justify doubling their budget.

Your room can also limit the benefits of expensive equipment. Walls, floors, furniture and speaker placement all affect how sound travels, especially at lower frequencies. Before spending hundreds on newly introduced equipment, try repositioning your speakers or changing where you sit; small changes to your audio setup can pay off.

Sources indicate that if you're looking for clearer dialogue and better everyday TV audio, you probably don't need to spend more than $150 to $200. A basic 2.1 soundbar gives you fuller sound and deeper bass without taking up much space. Inexpensive soundbars will work particularly well in small and medium-sized rooms, which makes them a practical choice if you aren't looking for a full home theater experience.

Industry observers note that if you watch a lot of movies or listen to music through your TV, spending around $250 to $500 gives you more options. This is where you can start finding dedicated center channels, Wi-Fi streaming and, depending on the model, physical rear speakers or Dolby Atmos.

Spending $500 to $1,000 or more makes sense if you want a more complete home theater experience, have a larger room or care about getting the most out of movies, games and music. At this level, you can find high-quality soundbars with multiple height channels, room correction and more customization options. You can also start building a component-based system, giving you more flexibility to upgrade over time.

Industry observers note that just remember that a higher price doesn't automatically mean a better fit. Consider your room, listening habits and the features you'll actually use before deciding how much to spend.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I hate running out of power.
  • It has been revealed that most folks should buy one of the first four power banks I recommend, but there are a few other unique use cases, so I’ve included a few extra options.
  • Updated November 2026: I added power banks from Anker, Peak Design, Nitecore, and Iniu, removed some older devices, and updated links and prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I hate running out of power. Everybody does. While our gadgets have advanced in many ways, battery technology has been slow to improve. That’s why you’re looking to buy a power bank. A good portable charger is a handy backup that can keep your smartphone, tablet, and maybe even your laptop going for longer. I’ve been testing power banks for years. I’ve tested more than 100 portable chargers. But you only really need one or two.

It has been revealed that most folks should buy one of the first four power banks I recommend, but there are a few other unique use cases, so I’ve included a few extra options. Read the Best MagSafe/Qi2 Power Banks for more magnetic wireless chargers, and Best Laptop Power Banks or Best Portable Power Stations for more power.

Updated November 2026: I added power banks from Anker, Peak Design, Nitecore, and Iniu, removed some older devices, and updated links and prices.

It has been revealed that this is the only power bank you need. Anker combines style and substance with this versatile power bank that packs a whopping 25,000-mAh capacity and is capable of delivering up to 165 watts to two devices (100 watts for a single device connected via USB-C). I love the rounded edges, the retractable, flat 2.3-foot USB-C cable up top, and the clever braided 1-foot USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop. It has a display to show the remaining battery, charging rate in and out, battery temperature, and health. It supports pass-through charging and takes around two hours to recharge.

It has been revealed that OK, you don’t really need this many stats, but having a precise idea of how much power remains is useful and reassuring. I love the built-in cables, because they ensure you’re never caught without one. This is also below the limit for power banks on flights, so you can travel with it. Anker’s Laptop Power Bank fast-charged everything I tested it with, including multiple smartphones, an iPad, a Poco tablet, a MacBook Air, and a Chromebook. You can charge four devices simultaneously without any issues. After a year of use, mine still performs perfectly.

You don’t always need massive capacity, and you don’t always have room for a big power bank. If you want something more portable, go for the Nimble Champ Pro. At 6.2 ounces, it’s one of the lightest on the market. It’s smaller than a deck of cards and can deliver 20 watts to charge two devices at once via a USB-C port on either end. It feels durable, comes in a snazzy new range of speckled color finishes, and has a bright lanyard loop that makes for easy carrying and helps you pick it out of your backpack. The Pro version is bigger but doubles the capacity (to 20,000 mAh) and has a similar design with two USB-C ports that go up to 65 watts. There’s also a smaller version with a 5,200-mAh capacity that tops out at 15 watts.

According to recent reports, another reason I like Nimble is its environmental efforts. Batteries are not environmentally benign. They use lithium, cobalt, and other rare metals whose supply chains are environmentally and socially questionable at best. But Nimble’s use of bioplastics and plastic-free minimal packaging at least reduces the environmental impact where it can be reduced. This version uses 90 percent recycled plastic (up 25 percent from the original) and comes in smaller plastic-free packaging. Nimble includes a 3.3-foot USB-C to USB-C cable in the box.

The original was the first Qi2 power bank I tested and was my top pick for quite a while, but this sequel is even better. The Qi2 wireless charging standard borrows elements of Apple’s MagSafe, enabling supported phones to connect with perfect alignment using a ring of magnets. Because it works with Apple's StandBy mode, you can stick Qi2 or MagSafe phones in portrait or landscape orientation.

According to recent reports, qi2 brings faster wireless charging rates of up to 25 watts, but it is also backward compatible, so older Qi devices can still charge (albeit more slowly). This compact portable charger has a handy kickstand, a two-way USB-C port on the left edge, and a power button with an LED display that can show remaining power as a percentage. It can also display charging time when plugged in, watts out, temperature, and battery health. Anker offers the device in a range of fun colors (I love the burgundy). Anker has added vents on top and bottom with a cooling fan you can turn off for silent mode. It is slimmer and lighter than the original and can charge faster, but it's also more expensive.

Despite a large capacity, it falls short of two full charges for your iPhone when charging wirelessly. You might squeeze out a little more if you plug in the short USB-C cable provided. It’s also quite bulky, but if you have an iPhone or another Qi2 phone, we recommend several slimmer alternatives in our Best Qi2 and MagSafe Power Banks guide.

Maybe you want a large-capacity power bank that can handle all your portable gadgets, but you’re tired of gray bricks. I am a sucker for Sharge’s transparent designs and cyberpunk aesthetic, but this prism-shaped power bank is more than just a pretty face. With a maximum output of 170 watts, a whopping 24,000-mAh capacity, and an IP66 rating for water resistance (fine in the rain, but best not to submerge), the Sharge 170 has form and function. The smart display shows battery life as a percentage, time remaining, and the input or output in watts. It supports many standards, including Power Delivery 3.1, Quick Charge 4.0, and PPS, and it fast-charged most of the devices I tested, including the iPhone 15 Pro, Pixel 8, Xiaomi 14 Ultra, and MacBook Air. You can simultaneously charge three devices at fast speeds.

Recent findings suggest that the box includes a braided USB-C cable and a somewhat pointless wee velvety bag (does anyone use these?). It can recharge completely in an hour via USB-C at up to 140 watts (with the right cable and charger). I’ve tested some of Sharge’s newer power banks, but I still prefer the 170. The triangular design is unique and means the display is always angled perfectly to glance at. You are paying a premium for the aesthetic, but I’ve used mine often over the last few months. It’s built to last.

My Apple Watch usually makes it to bedtime, but for super busy days and overnight trips, it’s nice to have a power bank capable of charging it up. This Anker power bank has a handy pop-up Apple Watch charger that can deliver 5 watts and supports Nightstand mode. It also has a built-in USB-C cable and a USB-C port, so you can deliver up to 30 watts to your phone or another small device. A display lights up beneath the surface to show you the remaining power as a percentage, and the current charging rate. It’s nice and compact, with a generous 10,000-mAh battery capacity, and comes in black, white, green, or pink. Anker supplies stickers to stop your Apple Watch from sliding, but I didn’t find that to be a problem.

It has been revealed that innovative and genuinely useful, I love the Nimble SharePower, a 10,000-mAh, modular power bank that you can snap in half to get two separate, fully functional 5,000-mAh chargers. This clever design allows you to share power with friends and family. The two halves connect magnetically with tiny pogo pins (it’s satisfying to pull them apart and reconnect). One has a built-in USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop, and the other has a fold-out USB-C connector. Put them together, and the remaining power is split evenly between the two halves. My daughter pinched this soon after it arrived in my home because it enables her to share the power with her friends, and I’m having trouble getting it back.

There are so many portable chargers out there. Here are a few more I like that just missed out on a place above for one reason or another. We also have separate guides for the Best Laptop Power Banks, Best MagSafe Power Banks, and Best Portable Power Stations.

Sources indicate that with its lovely textured finish and sleek design, this magnetic Qi2 power bank is a looker. It sticks to the back of your phone and charges wirelessly at 15 watts, also doubling as a stand for travel, thanks to its sturdy aluminum kickstand. When you plug it in via USB-C, it supports 25-watt wireless charging for your phone and pass-through charging, so it charges the battery at the same time. According to recent reports, this svelte, lightweight, 15,000-mAh power bank has a color display for stats and can deliver 65 watts across up to three devices. It has two USB-C ports and one USB-A, is fast to recharge (around 90 minutes at 100 watts), supports most fast-charging protocols and trickle charging for small devices, and is CCC certified for trips to China.

This model has a 2.3-foot retractable cable and the ability to charge devices at up to 45 watts.

Handmade by a small indie business in Brighton, England, from recycled plastic, Gomi claims at least 50 percent less CO2 emissions than other power banks.

It’s not fast, but this 10,000-mAh power bank has built-in USB-C and Lightning cables, USB-A and USB-C ports, and a handy display.

This is an affordable 20,000-mAh-capacity power bank with a cable that doubles as a carry loop. The USB-C cable and port can deliver a maximum of 67 watts (PD), and the USB-A can hit 22.5 watts, but those speeds drop if you charge multiple devices at once. It won’t fast-charge everything, and you won’t get the full capacity stated, but it’s a pretty good value.

Capable of delivering 300 watts, this power bank is close to the maximum capacity allowed on flights, and it can charge a couple of laptops and phones at the same time via the three USB-C ports (140W, 65W, 65W) and a retractable 2-foot USB-C cable (140W).

Looking like a power bank from the Nostromo, this can deliver a chart-topping 240 watts for two devices via the USB-C ports (140 watts and 100 watts), making it a good choice if you want to charge two laptops simultaneously.

Feature-packed with 26,250 mAh at 300 watts across two USB-C ports and one USB-A, a smart display and app control, and a 3.3-foot USB-C cable, this Anker Prime Power Bank is a beast.

Recent findings suggest that travel plug adapters cover trips to the UK, Europe, and Australia, among other places. It also has three ports and a magnetic Qi2 wireless charging pad.

You get slide-on Type C, I, and G plug adapters for travel, a magnetic wireless charger (up to 15 watts), USB-A and USB-C ports, and built-in USB-C and Lightning cables.

After extensive testing, this is our pick of the best portable jump starters, and it can charge gadgets at up to 65 watts via USB-C.

Small but mighty, this 10,000 mAh power bank is shock-, water-, and dustproof with an IP67 rating. A flap covers two USB-C ports, and there’s a ¼-inch thread for mounting—or you can screw in the supplied D-ring and use the carabiner to attach it to your bag. There’s even a small flashlight you can switch on by double-pressing the power button. It comes with a short braided USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop.

Thoughtfully designed power banks with an IP67 rating, built-in shock absorbers, and screw-on caps for the ports.

This portable charger has a whopping 90,000-mAh capacity, a pop-up lantern, and a versatile array of ports.

The Charge 100 Max can simultaneously charge up to five devices, and the wireless charging pad on top is handy in the dark when you don’t want to fumble with cables.

According to recent reports, this compact carbon fiber Nitecore power bank is the lightest I’ve tested with a 10,000-mAh capacity. It's also currently sold out.

iWalk Portable Charger for $22: The 4,800-mAh capacity won’t come close to fully refilling your device, but it's tiny enough to keep in a bag at all times.

What Features Should I Look for in Power Banks?

There are a few things worth thinking about when you’re shopping for a portable charger.

Recent findings suggest that the capacity of a power bank is measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), but this can be a little misleading because the amount of power you get depends on the cable you use, the device you’re charging, and the charging method. (Qi wireless charging is less efficient.) You will never get the maximum capacity from any power bank. You can generally expect to get between 60 and 80 percent after energy loss through heat and conversion. Some manufacturers list a “Rated Capacity” that’s lower than the overall capacity to give you an indication of what to expect in real-world use. We try to provide a minimum estimate of what you’ll get in terms of charges for devices.

It has been revealed that the charging rate for devices like smartphones is measured in watts (W), but most power banks list the voltage (V) and the amperage (A). Thankfully, you can calculate the wattage yourself simply by multiplying the voltage and amperage. Unfortunately, getting that maximum rate also depends on your device, the standards it supports, and the charging cable you use. Many smartphones, including Apple’s iPhones, support the power delivery standard, meaning you can use higher-power power banks to recharge the device with no challenges. A few phones, such as Samsung’s Galaxy S range, support a supplementary PD protocol called PPS (programmable power supply) that goes up to 45 watts. Many phones also support Qualcomm’s proprietary Quick Charge (QC) standard. There are also other proprietary fast-charging standards, but you won’t generally find power banks that support them unless they come from the smartphone manufacturer.

According to recent reports, your device will need pass-through support if you want to charge your power bank and use it to charge another device simultaneously. The Nimble, GoalZero, Biolite, Mophie, Zendure, and Sharge portable chargers listed support pass-through charging. Anker discontinued support for pass-through in some of its products because it found that differences between the output of the wall charger and the input of the device being charged can cause the power bank to cycle on and off rapidly and shorten its life. Monoprice does not support pass-through charging either. We would advise caution when using pass-through, as it can also cause portable chargers to heat up.

Can I Take a Power Bank on a Plane?

It’s safe to fly with a power bank, but there are two main restrictions to keep in mind when you board a flight: You must have the portable charger in your carry-on luggage (it cannot be checked), and it must not exceed 100 watt-hours. If your power bank has a larger capacity than 27,000 mAh, you should check with the airline. Below that should not be a problem.

Sources indicate that some airlines introduced stricter rules in 2025, so always check with your chosen airline before you travel. For example, some airlines prefer you not to use or charge power banks during a flight, some require power banks to be in your hand luggage under the seat in front of you and not in the overheads, and some limit the number of power banks you can have on board.

Why You Should Avoid Cheap Power Banks.

Many years ago, the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 gained notoriety when its batteries caught fire in a series of incidents. There’s been a steady stream of similar, though isolated, incidents ever since. Despite the high-profile coverage of batteries gone wrong, the vast majority of lithium-ion batteries are safe.

Recent findings suggest that the chemical reaction that occurs inside a lithium-ion cell is complex, but as in any battery, there’s a negative and a positive electrode. In lithium batteries, the negative is a lithium-carbon compound, and the positive is cobalt oxide (though many battery makers are moving away from cobalt). These two compounds cause a reaction that is safe when controlled and delivers energy to your devices. When the reaction gets out of control, though, you end up with earbuds melting in your ears. What changes a safe reaction to an uncontrolled reaction can be any number of things: excess heat, physical damage during use, physical damage during manufacture, or using the wrong charger.

The three basic rules that have kept me safe through testing dozens and dozens of batteries are these:.

It has been revealed that avoiding cheap wall-outlet adapters, cords, and chargers is the most important rule. These are your most likely sources of problems. Those chargers you see on Amazon for $20 cheaper than the competition? Not worth it. They probably got the price down by skimping on insulation, leaving out power-management tools, and ignoring the basics of electrical safety. Price alone is no guarantee of safety, either. Buy from reputable companies and brands.

Sources indicate that then there’s heat. Too much of it can cause all manner of problems, both in terms of discharge and safety. Avoid heat, and pay attention to your batteries when they’re charging. If your device gets overly hot when charging, this can be a sign of problems. Similarly, beware of any swollen, bulging, or otherwise misshapen batteries.

Why Is My Power Bank Charging Slowly?

It has been revealed that I’ve explained charging rates and capacity above, but several factors can cause charging speed to be slower than expected. The rate is determined by the device being charged, so your phone will request a certain wattage, which changes depending on how full its battery is, on-device settings, and the battery temperature.

Industry observers note that all devices charge more slowly when they are completely empty, when the battery approaches full, and when they overheat. The cable you use will also have a maximum charging rate, and so will different ports on the power bank. Wireless charging is more convenient, but also slower than wired charging.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been testing power banks for close to two decades, and my home office has stacks of ’em at any given moment. I test every portable charger that comes in for at least two weeks. I always check how many times it can fully charge my test phone (presently an iPhone 16). I’ll also try charging my Pixel 10 Pro XL and Samsung Galaxy S24+ to test charging speeds, and whatever else I have in. For larger-capacity power banks, I test-charge an iPad Mini and a MacBook Air. I test how long it takes to recharge each empty power bank.

Recent findings suggest that aside from these standard tests, I try to use the power banks in my everyday life, just to see how they feel, and my wife and kids often help out and share their opinions. For some of our top picks, I continue to test over months to get a sense of their reliability and durability, though it’s not possible to do this for every device that lands on my desk. Beyond function, I take form and usability into account. I keep an eye on user reviews and consider the warranties and customer service of each manufacturer.

How Does WIRED Select Power Banks to be Reviewed?

Sources indicate that I often scan the latest releases to seek out worthy prospects, whether from an unknown new brand or an established favorite like Anker. I also get pitched many power banks every week. I sometimes reach out to those companies to ask for the product but never promise any kind of editorial coverage—that would go against WIRED’s editorial policies. While WIRED usually earns affiliate revenue if you purchase a power bank using our link, this is not factored into the decision on ranking.

It has been revealed that there are too many power banks for me to test everything, so I tend to stick to known, reputable brands, but there’s always room for something new if it has a compelling new feature or price, and I cover as many as I can. (Leave a comment or send me an email if you want me to test a power bank from a certain brand!) Once testing is complete, I typically donate power banks to a local charity. I try to hang on to some of our top picks for comparison purposes and to test their longevity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

If you ask any Mac admin for a list of the software on their fleet, they’ll pull up their device management inventory and show you the apps they’ve deployed. Ask them what their developers installed with Homebrew last month, which VS Code extensions they are running, or what npm pulled into a project on Tuesday, and you’ll get a different response. That software was never procured by finance, never approved, and never inventoried. It’s also where a growing share of the risk lives in the AI era. Workbrew 2.0 treats that gap as a problem worth solving for IT teams.

According to recent reports, about Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

It has been revealed that device management is built around the software IT deploys. Apps from Apple Business Manager, apps preloaded via your device management vendors’ packages, packages you upload, and profiles you push out. That model solves the problem for native macOS apps. It doesn’t cover what happens when the Mac becomes the default developer machine. Developers install what they need with a single command in Terminal, and Homebrew alone has more than 16,000 packages. You then add millions of npm packages and hundreds of thousands of IDE extensions, and the list of software on a Mac that IT didn’t put there is longer than the list it did.

That used to be a developer-only problem. It isn’t anymore, in the vibe-coding era. AI tools have turned marketers, analysts, and ops people into builders, and those builders install packages too.

Workbrew started as a management layer for Homebrew: an agent that reports what’s installed, flags known vulnerabilities, and lets IT push updates across the fleet. Version 2.0 expands the catalog to include npm packages, VS Code extensions, and macOS apps, all in a single inventory. The firm claims it has patched more than 10 million vulnerabilities for customers since its launch, and it’s now ISO 27001-certified.

Industry observers note that the part that is critical for everyone who isn’t a developer is the new Workbrew app, a native Mac app for finding, installing, and updating approved software. Workbrew calls it “the app store for your entire tech giant.” Employees can browse what IT has approved, install it without opening Terminal, and request anything that isn’t on the list. IT approves or denies in the Workbrew Console, and if it’s a no, the employee gets an answer on why.

The app comes from the Updatest team, which Workbrew acquired as part of this release. Updatest is the indie Mac app that keeps thousands of users’ software up to date, and it remains a separate product for individuals and families. For business customer, that experience is now the Workbrew app, and it’s included on every blueprint, including the free Team plan with no device or user limits.

With Workbrew, we finally have real visibility into what developers are using in Homebrew. Fleet-wide updates are effortless, and the team stays secure without being slowed down.

Chris Merrell, Director of IT, End User Services, Camping World.

Recent findings suggest that workbrew isn’t a device management tool and isn’t trying to be one. Your device management system deploys the Workbrew agent, and Workbrew handles software your device management system lacks visibility into. How to use Gemini Notebook to turn your research into an interactive site

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • All you have to do is tell Gemini to make you a site using your sources.
  • Google's tagline for Gemini Notebook is "understand anything," because it's meant to help you better understand difficult concepts by creating study guides and even podcasts.
  • To use the service, tap or click on Create notebook and then upload your sources for any particular topic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

All you have to do is tell Gemini to make you a site using your sources.

Google's tagline for Gemini Notebook is "understand anything," because it's meant to help you better understand difficult concepts by creating study guides and even podcasts. Before it was called the Gemini Notebook, it was known as Google NotebookLM, which the company presented as its "deep research tool.".

To use the service, tap or click on Create notebook and then upload your sources for any particular topic. It accepts different types of sources, such as PDFs and images from your device or your Google Drive account. It also accepts links to websites, open source textbooks, books from the Play store and even copied text, such as your notes or emails. Gemini Notebook will then use those sources to create what you need, whether it's a study guide or a podcast featuring two AI hosts.

According to recent reports, gemini Notebook's latest feature can create a website you can interact with. Every website it makes has a unique design and comes with various elements, such as clickable sections, flash cards and quizzes that test whether you've learned anything from the information presented in it.

It has been revealed that it's incredibly easy to create an interactive site with Gemini Notebook. At the moment, the feature is live on desktop and available for all customers 18 years old and above. It is coming soon to the service's mobile app. But for now, you have to visit Gemini Notebook on the web and then hit New Notebook or Create notebook.

In the chat box within the new notebook's interface, type "make me a site" along with instructions on what you want the service to create for you. For the example above, I wrote: "Make a me site to help me understand the solar system and its elements. Explain them to me in simple sections with flash cards and create a quiz at the end." It will then draw information from your sources to make the website for you.

It has been revealed that if you don't have any sources uploaded, it will ask you if you want to do a web search to find the information you need. It could be good enough if you want to learn about known concepts and don't need the website to reflect details and data only you have access to. Gemini will let you know if your interactive site is done. You'll then be able to access the site in the Studio panel on the right-hand side of your screen. Just click or tap on the tab to load the site.

In my case, Gemini created a colorful website, with illustrations of the solar system and clickable sections, as you can see in the image above. Clicking on Mercury, for instance, shows a card with information about the smallest planet in our Solar System. It made separate sections for the four inner terrestrial planets, including Earth, and for the gas and ice giants in the outer Solar System. There are more clickable sections for the asteroid belt, the Kuiper belt and Oort cloud.

Sources indicate that maybe you read that last sentence and thought: "the? what?? cloud???" and rightly so! The Oort cloud is an entirely theoretical cluster of small, icy bodies past the Kuiper belt. Gemini presented it on this website as if it were extant and observed, describing it as "the home of long-period comets." The Kuiper belt was theorized decades before it was confirmed; that might end up being the case with the Oort cloud too. As with anything AI though, Gemini is not only capable of both hallucinating but of confidently misstating things too.

According to recent reports, in addition to creating easy-to-digest interactive websites to help you learn or prepare for exams, you can also use the new feature for other purposes. Google states you can use it to build project trackers for your job or dashboards that give you an overview of your sales, complete with visual aids.

SoftBank’s Son explored a $1tn SK Hynix buyout, The Information reports

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Masayoshi Son, chairman and chief executive of SoftBank Group.
  • SoftBank chief executive Masayoshi Son recently approached Wall Street institutions about financing a possible buyout of SK Hynix worth about $1tn, The Information reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.
  • SoftBank told The Information that Son is no longer pursuing the idea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Masayoshi Son, chairman and chief executive of SoftBank Group.

SoftBank chief executive Masayoshi Son recently approached Wall Street institutions about financing a possible buyout of SK Hynix worth about $1tn, The Information reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. Valida Pau, Phoebe Liu, Qianer Liu and Juro Osawa wrote the story.

SoftBank told The Information that Son is no longer pursuing the idea.

“SoftBank explores many opportunities, and this one is no longer under active consideration,” a SoftBank spokesperson told The Information.

Industry observers note that SK Hynix mentioned in a statement that it had no knowledge of the matter described in the report, Reuters reported. The chipmaker added that Korean law requires prior government approval for any foreign acquisition of the manufacturer. TNW has not independently verified the report.

Industry observers note that SK Hynix is now worth about 777 trillion won, or roughly $577.7bn, according to Seoul Economic Daily. That is well below the peak it reached about a month ago. The paper stated the $1tn figure reflects that peak value plus a 40% premium for control.

The memory maker first joined the trillion-dollar club in May, on demand for the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) that sits next to AI chips. In October it reported a 632% profit jump and mentioned the memory shortage would last until 2030.

It has been revealed that the Information set out why the deal faced long odds. It is unclear how SoftBank would pay, the outlet reported, because its OpenAI bets have already stretched its balance sheet. SoftBank completed its $30bn OpenAI investment in October.

According to recent reports, there is also no sign that the Wall Street firms would have lent the money. South Korea, like the US, tightly controls foreign takeovers of domestic technology. The Information judged it extremely unlikely that Seoul would let a Tokyo-based group lead a buyout of one of the country’s most vital tech assets. Nor is there any sign that SK Group, which controls SK Hynix, wanted to sell.

It has been revealed that memory is the one part of the AI supply chain SoftBank has not secured, Seoul Economic Daily reported. The group is the largest shareholder in chip designer Arm and owns server chip maker Ampere Computing and data centre investor DigitalBridge. It also holds large stakes in Intel and OpenAI. SK Hynix is one of three suppliers of HBM for AI accelerators, alongside Samsung Electronics and Micron.

Son has paid for his biggest bets with borrowed money. He funded the OpenAI stake by pledging Arm shares as collateral, the paper reported. This month SoftBank swung to a $7bn loss after writing off $3.7bn of AI power equipment.

It has been revealed that xiaomi introduced a second screen to its flagship phones with last year’s 17 Pros, but didn’t release them outside China. That means the newly introduced 18 Pro and Pro Max are the first chance I’ve had to find out if a screen on the back of a phone is any more useful now than it was when Xiaomi last tried it on 2021’s Mi 11 Ultra — not to mention earlier efforts by the likes of Nubia and Vivo.

It has been revealed that after a week or two with both of Xiaomi’s upcoming Pro phones, I’m not entirely sold. The rear display has a single, obvious use case — it’s helped me take some of the best selfies I’ve ever managed — but it isn’t very useful otherwise.

The rest of the phones are great, with good cameras, substantial batteries, and a more flexible take on the privacy display seen in the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. There’s a lot to like. But with prices higher than ever thanks to the RAM crisis, it’s hard not to wonder how much buyers are paying for a second screen they could probably do without.

Excellent main and telephoto camerasPrivacy displayStrong performanceCompact.

Rear display is limitedBasic ultrawide cameraExpensive.

Excellent main and telephoto camerasPrivacy displayStrong performanceExtended dynamic range.

Rear display is limitedBasic ultrawide cameraExpensive.

It has been revealed that there are two Xiaomi 18 Pro phones: the £1,199 Pro (around $1,570) and the £1,399 Pro Max (around $1,830). In the UK and Europe, they’re priced to compete directly with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

They come in similar sizes to the iPhones, too: a 6.4-inch display on the Pro, and 6.9 inches on the Pro Max. There are a few other differences, though not many. The Pro Max’s 7,050mAh battery is bigger than the Pro’s 6,000mAh (with larger batteries available outside Europe), and its 100W wired charging is 10W faster too. Both phones last a day pretty comfortably and will stretch to two with lighter use, though only just — I’ve seen better battery life from recent Oppo and Vivo flagships. They also use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips, though only the Pro Max has the Extreme version. And while the camera setups are nearly identical, you’ll get slightly better dynamic range from the bigger phone thanks to a LOFIC sensor.

Sources indicate that the rear screens also vary slightly in size between the phones, though at either 2.7 or 2.9 inches, there’s not much in it. Wrapping around the two main rear camera lenses, they look a lot like the displays you’ll find on the front of foldables like the Galaxy Z Flip 8, though smaller than most of those, and much more limited in functionality.

Industry observers note that you can set your choice of wallpapers, some of which are interactive. Listen to music or a podcast, and playback controls appear. You can turn on notifications, useful for when you want to rest your phone face down, but Xiaomi’s implementation is odd: App icons appear so large on the screen that there’s no space to fit much text from a given notification; there are no interactive responses like quick replies or marking emails as read; and you can’t see a list of your notifications, only viewing each for a few seconds as it comes in. It makes this just barely more useful than a notification LED.

In a recent development, unlike flip phones, you can’t use the small screen to access the phone’s settings, and you certainly can’t run full-blown apps. Instead, there’s a natural-language AI tool to create your own apps, powered by Google’s Gemini 4 Argon. It’s good for simple tools or games — I made a pomodoro timer and a semi-functional knockoff Pac-Man — but your creations can’t connect to the internet or access other apps, so anything you make will be quite purposefully limited.

In a recent development, the only thing that’s convinced me the rear screen is at all worthwhile is its camera viewfinder. The UI’s a little fiddly at this scale, but you can take photos, record videos, or create a photo booth-inspired picture set, all using the rear main camera. I’ve taken the best selfies of my life with this phone, which may be reason enough for some people to buy it.

It helps that the main camera is especially good. It and the telephoto are both excellent 200-megapixel shooters with large sensors, capable of great results in almost any lighting conditions. The telephoto’s short minimum focusing distance of 12cm lets it double as a great macro camera too. The 18 Pro Max has a slight photographic advantage, with a LOFIC main sensor that offers an expanded 16-stop dynamic range, helping it capture better highlights in particularly tricky lighting. Most of the time you won’t see a huge difference between the two phones.

Xiaomi’s longtime camera partner Leica is involved again, and by default you can shoot in one of two Leica-branded camera modes — Vibrant or Authentic — plus a fresh third option, the Xiaomi-branded Original, which splits the difference between them. The other substantial Leica contribution is a new Essential Moments mode that uses AI to simulate three different retro Leica aesthetics in either 35mm or 75mm lenses.

The ultrawide, set apart from the other two lenses beneath the screen, looks like an afterthought — and it shoots like one too. It’s placed so low on the body that my finger frequently blocks its view; its 17mm focal length barely feels wider than the 23mm main camera, so it doesn’t give you much extra room to play with; and its smaller sensor means quality is noticeably worse than from either of the other rear cameras, especially in dimmer light. As for the selfie camera, it’s decent, but you’ll only ever use it for video calls since the rear screen makes the main camera the better choice the rest of the time.

It has been revealed that the Xiaomi 18 Pro phones have one other trick: a privacy display. This is a pretty direct imitation of Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra tech, switching between different sets of pixels with varying viewing angles to make your screen hard to see from the side when it’s activated. Like Samsung’s version, you can turn it on across the phone or just for certain apps; unlike Samsung’s, when you activate it for specific apps, it also applies to specific notifications, and it works with split-screen or floating windows without affecting other apps open at the same time. It’s more flexible than Samsung’s version, though to my eye, less effective.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro and Pro Max have plenty of strengths, with great main and telephoto cameras, good performance, and reasonably attractive designs. But shortcomings like the lackluster ultrawide camera and batteries that don’t last as long as some rival flagships make me wonder about the compromises made to fit that rear display. Its limited functionality has given me pause, especially as flagship phones like this hit increasingly eye-watering prices.
